How to read this pageThe formal documents behind the project: audit engagement letter, audit report, EBIOS RM analysis, security policy, test reports, incident log, threat watch, operations manual. They are long on purpose: they are what another administrator would use.

Annex guide

The annexes are formal documents: they keep their original tone. Technical terms are in English, as in the rest of the report; the glossary (Annex L) gives the French term with its English equivalent. This guide gives the content of each annex.

Annex A · Audit engagement letter

Project: Hybrid InfraSec — Zero-Trust infrastructure of the company INFRASEC

Reference: LM-AUDIT-2026-01

Issue date: 01/10/2026

Sponsor: IT department (DSI), INFRASEC

Addressee: appointed audit team (internal audit carried out under the responsibility of the secure infrastructure administrator; this framework applies identically to a third-party provider)

Author / technical contact: admin (secure infrastructure administrator)

1. Context INFRASEC runs a target infrastructure segmented along Zero-Trust lines (single crossing point pfSense, Active Directory domain infrasec.local, TrueNAS storage, container node, Wazuh SIEM). Before putting a remote access evolution (WireGuard VPN) into production, and as part of keeping the systems secure (MCS), management wants an objective assessment of the security level of the scope.

This letter defines the mandate, scope, expected method, rules of engagement and deliverables of the audit. It also serves as the reference against which the audit report will be assessed.

2. Purpose and objectives Assess the security level of the INFRASEC infrastructure and provide a usable report to decide on treatment measures. Objectives:

  • identify the vulnerabilities and exposures of the components in scope;
  • characterise the related risks and threats (criticality);
  • measure the gap with good practice (ANSSI, CIS);
  • make prioritised remediation recommendations;
  • feed the risk analysis (EBIOS Risk Manager) and the ISSP.

3. Scope

In scope:

ComponentAddressType of check
pfSense (firewall / gateway)10.10.10.254exposure, filtering rules, admin interface
Win-Server-DC (AD DS / DNS)10.10.10.10exposed services, hardening, account policy
TrueNAS (storage / SMB)10.10.10.20exposed services, shares, AD join
fedora (container node)10.10.10.30system hardening, SSH, rootless containers
wazuh-siem (SIEM)10.10.10.40exposure, configuration
Segment10.10.10.0/24exposure mapping, segmentation

Out of scope: the physical virtualisation host, the upstream home network, client devices, simulated public cloud services. Any extension of the scope requires a written amendment.

4. Regulatory framework and references The audit takes into account:

  • the ANSSI recommendations (hygiene and hardening guides);
  • the GDPR for the protection of personal data (processing scope);
  • a risk management method of the EBIOS Risk Manager / ISO 27005 type;
  • the CIS configuration benchmarks (through the Lynis tool);
  • the MITRE ATT&CK framework to qualify threats.

6. Rules of engagement

  • Authorised time window: on the mock-up, with no production constraint.
  • Explicit authorisation from the sponsor for active tests (scanning, controlled authentication attempt).
  • Non-destructive: no deliberate alteration of data; no unplanned service interruption.
  • No exfiltration of real data; work on lab data.
  • Single point of contact: the technical contact, reachable throughout the window.
  • Confidentiality: findings are treated as sensitive and are not shared outside the agreed scope.

7. Expected deliverables 1. Audit report presenting the control points, the measurements taken and the assessment of the security level.

2. List of vulnerabilities identified, rated by severity, with a remediation recommendation and treatment phase.

3. Characterisation of the related risks and threats (MITRE ATT&CK mapping where relevant).

4. Integrity register (SHA-256) of the deliverables produced.

The report must be clear, structured and usable by someone who did not carry out the audit.

8. Criteria for assessing the work The audit report will be considered compliant if it:

  • covers the whole scope defined in §3;
  • applies the methodology of §5;
  • identifies the vulnerabilities and characterises the risks (§2);
  • provides prioritised, actionable recommendations;
  • complies with the rules of engagement of §6;
  • complies with the distribution policy of §9.

9. Confidentiality and distribution The deliverables contain no public IP address, real MAC address, authentication secret or personal data. The addressing plan uses RFC 1918 private ranges (10.10.10.0/24). Documents are sealed with a SHA-256 hash.

Annex B · Security audit report (PV-02)

Project: Hybrid InfraSec — Zero-Trust lab

Scope: segment 10.10.10.0/24, pfSense chokepoint, 5 assets (pfSense, DC, TrueNAS, fedora, Wazuh) + hypervisor

Audit date: 04/10/2026

Auditor: admin

Audit workstation: node fedora (10.10.10.30) — administration/audit workstation. In production, a dedicated hardened workstation (Parrot/Kali) would separate the roles.

1. Methodology Audit in three complementary layers:

1. Network exposure mapping — service and OS scan (nmap -sS -sV -O) over the whole segment.

2. System hardening — CIS audit of the Linux hosts (Lynis 3.1.7).

3. Configuration compliance — Wazuh's native Security Configuration Assessment (SCA), already active on the Windows (DC) and Linux (fedora) agents.

Tools: nmap 7.92, Lynis 3.1.7, Wazuh 4.14 (SCA module).

2. Layer 1 — Exposure mapping (nmap) 6 active hosts detected. Exposure surface per asset:

Strengths observed:

  • On each host, most of the 1,000 ports tested are filtered: the scan, run from the segment, does not cross pfSense, so this filtering comes from the hosts' local firewalls. pfSense itself only exposes DNS resolution and its administration interfaces (including HTTP :80, finding F-02).
  • No dangerous legacy or unencrypted service (no Telnet, FTP, SMBv1).
  • TLS available on the administration interfaces (443, Cockpit 9090, Grafana, Wazuh dashboard), except pfSense's HTTP :80 listener (F-02).

3. Layer 2 — System hardening (Lynis / fedora)

  • Hardening index: 69/100 (253 tests run)
  • Warnings: 0
  • Suggestions: 20 (areas for improvement, no critical defect)

Main suggestions:

  • SSH (SSH-7408): AllowTcpForwarding → NO, ClientAliveCountMax → 2, LogLevel → VERBOSE.
  • Password policy (AUTH-9230/9286): set PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_MAX_DAYS, hashing rounds in /etc/login.defs.
  • umask (AUTH-9328): set the default value to 027.
  • Unneeded network protocols (NETW-3200): disable dccp, sctp, rds, tipc.
  • Removable storage drivers (USB-1000, STRG-1846): disable USB/FireWire storage if not needed.
  • Automatic updates (PKGS-7420): enable dnf-automatic.
  • Disk partitioning (FILE-6310): separate partitions for /home and /var.

4. Layer 3 — Configuration compliance (Wazuh SCA) Wazuh's Security Configuration Assessment module continuously checks the agents against CIS benchmarks:

  • DC01 (Windows Server 2025) — CIS Microsoft Windows Server benchmark.
  • fedora (Linux) — CIS Distribution Independent Linux benchmark.

Evidence: Wazuh dashboard → "Configuration Assessment" module (screenshots kept offline by the auditor). Benefit: Windows coverage where Lynis does not apply.

6. Security measures already in place (strengths)

  • Single chokepoint pfSense with default deny filtering between zones; inside the segment, filtering relies on the hosts' local firewalls.
  • Monitoring: Wazuh SIEM (events + SCA + FIM) with agents on the domain controller and the fedora node, and Prometheus/Grafana metrics on both hosts.
  • Rootless containers (Podman) on the fedora node — no root daemon, reduced surface.
  • Backup designed on 3-2-1-0, restore verified (PV-01) — ZFS snapshots + replication + SHA-256 check.
  • Encryption in transit (TLS) on the administration interfaces, except pfSense's HTTP :80 listener (F-02).
  • AD integration with NFSv4 ACLs on the file share (centralised access control).

7. Conclusion The lab shows a sound security posture (hardening index 69/100, no dangerous legacy service, effective firewall, full monitoring). The findings are mostly of low to medium severity and fall under incremental hardening; the three priority findings were decided on during the freeze phase: F-01 accepted temporarily with a compensating measure, F-02 and F-03 planned (see the freeze report). The related risk analysis is developed in the EBIOS Risk Manager document, and the organisational measures in the ISSP.

Appendices: full nmap output (/tmp/nmap-infrasec_20261004.txt), Lynis report (/var/log/lynis- report.dat), Wazuh SCA screenshots.

2. Gap identified A single partial gap: the engagement letter mentions Kali-type audit tools. The dedicated vulnerability scanner (OpenVAS) could not be used — the prebuilt audit machine did not boot. Coverage was ensured another way: nmap scan for exposure, Lynis for hardening, Wazuh SCA for configuration, and a controlled brute-force test for detection (PV-03). The goal of the engagement letter — identify and rate the vulnerabilities — is met; only the method of one tool differs.

Treatment: adding an OpenVAS/GVM scan is recorded as an improvement for the next audit cycle. It does not call the established findings into question.

3. Overall verdict The audit report (PV-02) is assessed as compliant with the engagement letter LM-AUDIT-2026-01. All requirements on scope, method, deliverables, rules of engagement and distribution are met. The single gap (dedicated vulnerability scanning tool) is partial, justified, has no impact on the validity of the findings, and is the subject of a recorded improvement action.

Annex D · EBIOS Risk Manager risk analysis

AIS certification lab "Hybrid InfraSec" — Zero-Trust architecture

(ANSSI, 2018 edition)

Type of deliverableFormal security assessment document — presented to a jury
Date4 October 2026
Authoradmin — secure infrastructure administrator (security analyst role)
ReferencesEBIOS RM (ANSSI), MITRE ATT&CK, ANSSI IT hygiene guide, ISO/IEC

Input documents reusedPV-01 (backup / RTO validation), PV-02 (configuration audit — findings

Confidentiality notice — This document describes an isolated lab environment. No public IP address, real authentication secret or personal data appears in this deliverable. The addresses mentioned belong to the lab's private RFC 1918 addressing plan.

Summary for the jury (executive summary) The "Hybrid InfraSec" lab implements a hybrid virtualisation infrastructure (KVM/libvirt on Fedora 44) organised around a single crossing point — the pfSense firewall — following a Zero-Trust approach. It hosts an Active Directory trust core (infrasec.local), ZFS storage (TrueNAS), a rootless Podman container node monitored by Prometheus/Grafana, and a Wazuh 4.14 SIEM for detection (SCA, FIM, correlation).

The EBIOS RM assessment below identifies four business values (directory and authentication service, integrity/availability of stored data, monitoring and detection chain, business continuity) and six supporting assets. The most severe feared events (severity G4 — Critical) are the compromise of the Active Directory forest and the malicious encryption (ransomware) of the SMB shares.

The PV-02 audit findings (F-01 to F-11) are used as proven vulnerabilities feeding the operational scenarios. The two structural vulnerabilities are the presence of the hypervisor's administration plane on the production segment (F-01) and the exposure of RDP to the whole segment (F-03), which open high-likelihood attack paths.

The treatment plan (workshop 5) relies on the measures already in place (Wazuh, pfSense, 3-2-1-0 backup with RTO < 1 s, rootless containers) and on the prioritised remediation of the PV-02 findings. Once the plan is applied, no risk remains in the critical zone (target; to date, hardening is partly applied and segmentation M-01 to M-04 is planned); the residual risks are considered acceptable, provided the short-term measures are followed up.

Workshop 1 — Framing and security baseline

1.1 Purpose of the workshop Define the study framework, identify the business values and supporting assets, formalise the related feared events with their severity, then assess the gap between the expected security baseline and the real state of the environment.

1.2 Business and technical scope

Business scope The "Hybrid InfraSec" lab aims to demonstrate control of a hardened Zero-Trust architecture combining enterprise infrastructure services (directory, files), a containerised DevSecOps chain and security monitoring. The "mission" of the system is to provide and prove:

  • a centralised authentication and authorisation service (Active Directory, RBAC);
  • a resilient, backed-up file storage service;
  • an observability and incident detection chain (metrics + SIEM);
  • business continuity (3-2-1-0 backup, controlled RTO).

Technical scope Single-segment virtualised infrastructure with a single chokepoint.

Workshop 1 conclusion — The architecture has a consistent baseline (chokepoint, RBAC, backup, SIEM) but three structural gaps (F-01, F-03, F-06) weaken the claimed Zero-Trust model: the administration plane is not segmented and sensitive accesses (hypervisor, RDP) are exposed to the whole segment.

Workshop 2 — Risk sources and targeted objectives

2.1 Purpose of the workshop Identify the relevant Risk Source (SR) / Targeted Objective (OV) pairs with regard to the business values, then assess them to keep the highest-priority ones for the rest of the study.

2.2 Assessment criteria

  • Motivation: interest of the SR in reaching the OV (low / medium / high).
  • Resources: technical, financial and human capabilities (limited / medium / high).
  • Activity / relevance: plausibility with regard to the lab's scope.

Each pair receives an overall relevance: Not very relevant / Relevant / Very relevant.

2.4 Justification of the selection

  • SR-1 (cybercriminal/ransomware): the dominant threat today; directly targets the SMB shares and AD. Top priority.
  • SR-2 (script kiddie): services exposed without authentication (F-05 node-exporter, F-04 WS-Discovery, F-02 clear HTTP) are low-effort targets. Relevant given the proven vulnerabilities.
  • SR-3 (insider): an operator with legitimate access (RDP open to the whole segment, SSH/Cockpit reachable) can abuse their rights. Relevant.
  • SR-4 (APT): kept as a robustness benchmark but ruled out as a priority scenario (the lab has no espionage value). It is not turned into an operational scenario.
  • SR-5 (supply chain): the DevSecOps chain (container images) introduces an external dependency. Relevant and current.

Pairs kept for workshops 3 and 4: SR-1, SR-2, SR-3, SR-5.

Workshop 5 — Risk treatment

5.1 Purpose of the workshop Define the continuous security improvement plan (PACS), derive the measures from the existing controls and the remediation of the PV-02 findings, then assess the residual risks and produce the before/after map.

5.2 Treatment strategy The strategy chosen is risk reduction (lowering likelihood through segmentation and authentication), backed by a restored Zero-Trust posture. Transfer does not apply (lab); avoidance is not desirable (the services are the lab's mission); acceptance is reserved for low residual risks or, for a high residual risk whose severity is intrinsic, for an explicit decision by the CISO: justified, backed by detection and recovery measures, dated and reviewed periodically.

Main residual risk — Even after treatment, SO-1 and SO-2 keep a G4 severity (intrinsic to the trust core) with likelihood brought down to V2. They are accepted because: (1) the 3-2-1-0 backup guarantees continuity (ER-2), and (2) Wazuh detection ensures reactivity. Quarterly follow-up of detection effectiveness is recommended.

Reading — Treatment moves the three critical scenarios out of column V3: SO-3 goes to V1 (segmented admin plane), SO-1 and SO-2 to V2 (access restriction + detection). No scenario remains in the critical zone (G4×V3/V4). The residual risks sit between the "controlled high" and "moderate" zones.

General conclusion The EBIOS RM assessment of the "Hybrid InfraSec" lab confirms the relevance of the targeted Zero-Trust architecture, while objectively measuring the gap between the stated intent and the audited configuration (PV-02, Lynis 69/100). The three critical risks identified — ransomware on the SMB share (SO-1), compromise of Active Directory through RDP (SO-2) and pivot to the hypervisor (SO-3) — all stem from a lack of segmentation of the administration plane and overly broad access (F-01, F-03, F-06).

The proposed treatment plan relies first on the measures already present (3-2-1-0 backup with RTO < 1 s, Wazuh SIEM, rootless Podman, pfSense chokepoint) and on targeted, low-cost remediations (dedicated administration network, RDP restriction, SMB micro-segmentation, TLS everywhere, service authentication). Implementing them brings every scenario out of the critical risk zone, restoring the consistency of the Zero-Trust model and raising the infrastructure to a maturity level in line with the AIS certification.

Article 1 — Purpose, scope and reach

1.1 Purpose

1.1.1 This Information Systems Security Policy (hereafter "ISSP") defines all the rules, guiding principles and technical and organisational requirements that apply to the AIS certification lab "Hybrid InfraSec".

1.1.2 The purpose of the ISSP is to guarantee, in a verifiable and auditable way, the following security properties across the whole scope:

  • Confidentiality: information is accessible only to authorised entities.
  • Integrity: data, configurations and logs cannot be altered in an unauthorised or undetected way.
  • Availability: services and data are accessible according to the continuity objectives defined in Article 8.
  • Traceability / accountability: every significant action is logged and attributable to an identity.
  • Evidence: the elements needed for audit and litigation are kept and protected.

1.2 Technical scope

1.2.1 The scope covers the whole infrastructure hosted on the physical host TeneT and its hosting network:

ComponentHost / RoleAddressMain functions

administration

DHCP

1.2.2 The lab's single network segment is 10.10.10.0/24. All traffic entering or leaving the segment MUST go through the single crossing point (chokepoint) pfSense (10.10.10.254). Inside the segment, flows between machines do not cross pfSense: they are restricted by the hosts' local filtering (see 6.3).

1.3 Organisational scope and reach

1.3.1 The ISSP applies to:

  • the lab operator and anyone with access (administrator, auditor, jury member during assessment);
  • all the hardware, software, virtual, containerised and information assets listed in Article 4;
  • any third-party provider or tool working on the scope.

1.3.2 Any exception to a rule of this ISSP MUST be the subject of a formal, justified request, recorded, limited in time and approved by the CISO. Active exceptions MUST be listed in the exceptions register (Addendum E.3) and reviewed at each audit cycle.

1.3.3 Failure to comply with the ISSP rules is a non-compliance that may lead to the immediate suspension of the access concerned and, where applicable, to failing the certification.

Article 2 — Framework and normative references

2.1 Alignment principle

2.1.1 The ISSP aligns, as a methodological reference, with the frameworks below. Since the lab is a training certification environment, this alignment aims at consistency and verifiability, with no claim to formal certification against the frameworks cited.

2.3 Guiding principles

2.3.1 The whole ISSP is governed by the following guiding principles, which prevail whenever a rule is ambiguous:

1. Zero-Trust — No implicit trust is granted based on network location. Every request is authenticated, authorised and checked.

2. Least privilege — Each identity, service or container only has the rights strictly needed for its function.

3. Defence in depth — Security measures are layered (network, system, container, application, data) so that no single failure compromises the scope.

4. Secure by default — Delivered configurations are restrictive (deny by default); opening is the justified exception.

5. Full traceability — Every administration or security action is logged centrally and timestamped.

6. Encryption in transit — Any flow carrying authentication, administration or sensitive data MUST be encrypted (TLS, SSH or WireGuard).

Article 3 — Security organisation and governance

3.1 Roles and responsibilities

3.1.1 Security governance relies on a separation of roles. One person MAY hold several roles in this single-operator lab, but actions MUST remain traceable by distinct functional role (dedicated accounts — see Article 5).

3.1.2 The principle of segregation of duties MUST be respected in spirit: the entity that runs a service MUST NOT be the only one to check its own logs. The audit function and SIEM monitoring MUST have independent read access that operations administrators cannot modify.

3.2 Security committee and review

3.2.1 A security review MUST be held at least at the end of each audit cycle and after any major incident. It covers: the state of risks, incidents, active exceptions, SCA/FIM results, the state of backups and the improvement plan.

3.2.2 The review's decisions MUST be recorded in a dated decision log kept as evidence.

3.3 Documentation and upkeep

3.3.1 The ISSP, the related procedures and the registers (assets, exceptions, incidents, secrets) MUST be kept up to date and versioned.

3.3.2 Any change to the ISSP MUST be approved by the CISO, traced (version, date, reason) and communicated to the roles concerned.

Article 4 — Asset classification and management

4.1 Asset inventory

4.1.1 A complete asset inventory MUST be kept up to date. No asset (virtual machine, container, share, ZFS pool, service account) MAY exist outside the inventory.

4.1.2 Each asset MUST have an owner (responsible role), a classification level and a criticality level.

4.4.2 Media and datasets holding C2 or C3 data MUST be securely erased (destruction of the ZFS datasets and their snapshots) before reuse or disposal.

Article 5 — Identity and access management

5.1 Principles

5.1.1 The single authentication and authorisation authority of the scope is Active Directory (forest infrasec.local), carried by Win-Server-DC. Resources that can be joined to the domain (e.g. TrueNAS SMB shares) MUST rely on Active Directory RBAC.

5.1.2 The principle of least privilege MUST apply to every identity. Rights are granted through group membership, never directly to an individual on the resources.

5.1.3 Every action MUST be attributable to a named identity. Shared generic accounts ARE FORBIDDEN, except explicitly listed service accounts (see 5.4).

5.3 Privileged accounts

5.3.1 Domain administration accounts (e.g. members of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins) MUST be strictly limited and named, and MUST NOT be used for everyday tasks or browsing.

5.3.2 Administration MUST follow the tiering principle: highly privileged accounts MUST NOT be exposed on less trusted machines. The administration plane is restricted according to Article 6.

5.3.3 Privileged accounts MUST be disabled as soon as they are no longer needed and reviewed at each audit cycle.

5.4 Service accounts

5.4.1 Each service (SMB domain join, Wazuh agent, metrics exporter, etc.) MUST have a dedicated service account, documented in the inventory, with the minimum scope of rights.

5.4.2 Service accounts MUST NOT have interactive logon rights when these are not required.

5.4.3 Passwords of multi-platform service accounts (Windows / Linux / NAS) MUST use characters that type identically across keyboard layouts to avoid input errors between platforms, while keeping high entropy (see 5.5).

5.5 Password policy and multi-factor authentication

5.5.1 The password policy is set by GPO on the domain and MUST meet at least:

SettingRequirement
Minimum length (user accounts)14 characters
Minimum length (privileged /
service accounts)		20 characters
ComplexityUpper case, lower case, digits and special characters
Keyboard compatibility (multi-platform accounts)Characters typed identically on the target
layouts
HistoryLast 24 passwords cannot be reused
LockoutAfter 5 failed attempts, over a 15-minute window
Rotation of privileged / service accountsAt least every 90 days and at any suspicion of compromise
StorageNever in clear; see Article 11

5.5.2 Multi-factor authentication (MFA) SHOULD be enabled for any administration access where the component allows it (e.g. pfSense interface, Cockpit access through a compatible solution). Where MFA is not natively available, the compensation MUST be documented (network restriction of the administration plane, high-entropy passwords, stricter rotation).

5.5.3 The default passwords of every component (pfSense, TrueNAS, Grafana, Wazuh, Cockpit) MUST be changed at installation.

5.6 Access life cycle

5.6.1 Any creation, change or removal of access MUST be traced and justified.

5.6.2 A review of accounts and group memberships MUST be carried out at each audit cycle to detect dormant or excessive rights.

Article 6 — Network security and segmentation

6.1 Single crossing point (chokepoint)

6.1.1 The pfSense firewall (10.10.10.254) is the single, mandatory crossing point for all flows entering or leaving the segment, including WireGuard remote access. It acts as gateway, DNS resolver, DHCP server and filter.

6.1.2 No flow MAY bypass the chokepoint. Any alternative route, unauthorised tunnel or extra network interface on a VM is a non-compliance and MUST be removed.

6.2 Deny by default filtering

6.2.1 The filtering policy MUST follow the deny by default principle: any flow not explicitly allowed is blocked.

6.2.2 Allow rules MUST be named (source, destination, port, protocol, justification) and listed. Any obsolete rule MUST be removed.

6.2.3 Reference matrix of allowed flows (any missing line is forbidden):

6.3 Segmentation and micro-segmentation

6.3.1 Although the lab relies on a single segment 10.10.10.0/24, the Zero-Trust principle MUST be applied through logical micro-segmentation: flows entering or leaving the segment are filtered by pfSense; communications between VMs in the segment, which do not cross pfSense, are restricted by host filtering (local rules) to the strict minimum defined in 6.2.3, pending the dedicated administration network (EBIOS measure M-01).

6.3.2 Communications between VMs MUST NOT be allowed globally. The absence of an explicit rule means prohibition, including for machines in the same subnet.

6.4 Restricting the administration plane (Zero-Trust)

6.4.1 The administration interfaces (Cockpit on TeneT, pfSense console, TrueNAS interface, Grafana, Wazuh dashboard) MUST NOT be exposed to the whole segment. Access to them MUST be restricted to explicitly authorised administration-plane sources.

6.4.2 Any administration access MUST be encrypted (TLS / HTTPS / SSH). Clear-text administration protocols (HTTP, Telnet) ARE FORBIDDEN.

6.4.3 Administration services MUST NOT listen on unneeded interfaces or addresses.

6.5 Network services

6.5.1 Internal DNS resolution is provided by Win-Server-DC for the infrasec.local zone and relayed/filtered through pfSense. Unauthorised resolvers ARE FORBIDDEN.

6.5.2 The DHCP server runs exclusively on pfSense. Any other DHCP service on the segment is a non-compliance (rogue DHCP risk).

Article 7 — Hardening of systems and containers

7.1 System hardening

7.1.1 All systems (TeneT, Linux VMs, Win-Server-DC) MUST be hardened according to the applicable CIS Benchmarks and the ANSSI hygiene guides.

7.1.2 Unneeded services, accounts and software MUST be disabled or removed (attack surface reduction).

7.1.3 File permissions MUST follow least privilege. Using chmod 777 (or any mode granting write access to everyone) IS FORBIDDEN. Rights MUST be controlled through an appropriate owner (chown), dedicated groups and, for containers, user namespaces.

7.1.4 A recovery snapshot (Snapper / ZFS) MUST be taken before any major operation (update, structural configuration change, deployment) to allow a quick rollback.

7.2 Container hardening (rootless OCI)

7.2.1 Containers MUST run in rootless OCI mode by default (Podman) on the fedora node. Isolation MUST rely on user namespaces.

7.2.2 Any need for root privilege, a privileged container or the exposure of a privileged port (< 1024) MUST be justified in writing, approved by the CISO and listed in the exceptions register. Without justification, such configurations ARE FORBIDDEN.

7.2.3 Container images MUST come from trusted sources, be versioned (no systematic use of latest in operations) and be scanned for vulnerabilities before deployment.

7.2.4 Containers MUST apply least privilege: removal of unneeded Linux capabilities, read-only file systems where possible, and no clear-text secret in the image or in persisted environment variables (see Article 11).

7.2.5 Summary of container rules:

RuleRequirement
Execution modeRootless (Podman) by default
IsolationUser namespaces mandatory
Root / privilegedForbidden unless a justified, approved exception
Port < 1024Forbidden unless a justified, approved exception
chmod 777 in volumesForbidden (use chown + groups)
Image originTrusted sources, pinned tag, scanned
Linux capabilitiesReduced to the strict minimum
SecretsNever in clear (see Art. 11)

7.3 Vulnerability and update management

7.3.1 Systems and images MUST be watched and analysed for vulnerabilities regularly. Wazuh's SCA (Security Configuration Assessment) module MUST be enabled on the agents to assess compliance with the hardening baselines.

7.3.2 Security patches MUST be applied within delays proportionate to criticality: at once for an actively exploited critical vulnerability affecting a vital asset; in the planned maintenance cycle for the others.

7.3.3 Every update MUST be preceded by a recovery snapshot (see 7.1.4) and followed by a functional check.

Article 8 — Data protection, backup and continuity

8.1 Protection of data at rest and in transit

8.1.1 C2 and C3 data MUST be protected. Encryption at rest SHOULD be applied to sensitive TrueNAS datasets where the platform allows it (native ZFS encryption).

8.1.2 Any transport of authentication, administration or sensitive data MUST be encrypted in transit (TLS/signed SMB/secure NFS/SSH/HTTPS).

8.2 Data access control (ACL)

8.2.1 TrueNAS SMB shares MUST be joined to the infrasec.local domain and their access governed by Active Directory RBAC through groups.

8.2.2 NFSv4 ACLs MUST be defined on least privilege, avoiding any broad permission (everyone / world write access). Using chmod 777 on shared datasets IS FORBIDDEN (see 7.1.3).

8.3 3-2-1-0 backup strategy

8.3.1 The backup strategy MUST follow the 3-2-1-0 model:

DigitMeaningImplementation in the lab
33 copies of the dataProduction data + local ZFS snapshot + replication
22 different storage mediaSeparate replication target (tank/partage_backup);
second physical medium in production (in the lab, same
pool: see PV-01)
11 off-site / isolated copyReplication to a remote site in production (not reached in
the lab: see PV-01)
00 verified errorsIntegrity check with a SHA-256 hash

8.3.2 The mechanisms MUST include: scheduled ZFS snapshots, replication of the snapshots to a separate target, and integrity checks with a SHA-256 hash after each replication.

8.3.3 Restore MUST be tested periodically (documented restore test), since a backup that cannot be restored has no value.

8.4 Continuity objectives (RPO / RTO) and DRP

8.4.1 The recovery objectives per asset class are:

8.4.2 A disaster recovery plan (DRP, French PRA) MUST document the restart order (pfSense chokepoint, then AD, then dependent services), the restore procedures and the people responsible. The DRP MUST be tested at least once per cycle.

8.4.3 Snapshots and replications MUST be monitored; any failure MUST raise an alert handled according to Article 10.

Article 9 — Logging, monitoring and detection

9.1 Centralised logging

9.1.1 All assets in scope MUST send their logs to the central Wazuh SIEM (wazuh- siem, 10.10.10.40) through an agent or a dedicated flow. Status on 11/10/2026: agents deployed on Win- Server-DC and fedora; connecting pfSense, TrueNAS and the hypervisor to the SIEM remains to be done (tracked gap).

9.1.2 Logs MUST NOT be modifiable or deletable by the operations administrators of the monitored machines. Integrity and retention are managed on the SIEM side.

9.1.3 The clocks of all systems MUST be synchronised (common time reference) to guarantee consistent correlations.

9.2 Logging policy

9.2.1 At least the following events MUST be logged and forwarded:

SourceEvents loggedPurpose
Win-Server-DC
(AD)		Authentications (success/failure), changes to
accounts/groups, privilege escalations, GPOs		RBAC traceability, abuse
detection
pfSenseBlocked/allowed flows, rule changes, VPN/admin
events		Chokepoint monitoring
TrueNASShare access, ACL changes, ZFS errors,
snapshots/replication		Data integrity and access
fedora / containersContainer start/stop, privilege use,
Podman events		Container abuse detection
TeneT / CockpitAdmin logons, libvirt actions, snapshotsHypervisor monitoring
wazuh-siemAlerts, SCA, FIM, agent statusDetection and compliance

9.2.2 The retention period of logs MUST be at least 90 days online for security logs, and longer for events linked to an open incident (kept until closure and lessons learned). Logs MUST remain usable and protected throughout the retention period.

9.3 Detection (SCA, FIM)

9.3.1 Wazuh's SCA (Security Configuration Assessment) module MUST be enabled to continuously assess the systems' compliance with the hardening baselines (Article 7).

9.3.2 The FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) module MUST watch the integrity of sensitive files and folders (configurations, critical binaries, ACL files) and raise an alert on any unexpected change.

9.3.3 Detection rules MUST be maintained and tuned to limit false positives while covering the relevant threat scenarios (privilege escalation, lateral movement, log tampering, unjustified creation of a privileged port).

9.4 Operational monitoring

9.4.1 Metrics are monitored by Prometheus (collection through node-exporter and windows_exporter) and displayed by Grafana on the fedora node; the firewall is monitored over SNMP by Zabbix.

9.4.2 Alert thresholds MUST be set for vital indicators (service availability, resource saturation, snapshot/replication failure, loss of a Wazuh agent). Loss of an agent's reporting MUST be handled as a security event.

Article 10 — Security incident management

10.1 Definition and detection

10.1.1 A security incident is any event that actually or potentially harms the confidentiality, integrity, availability or traceability of the scope.

10.1.2 Detection relies mainly on Wazuh (alerts, SCA, FIM), Prometheus/Grafana monitoring and pfSense logs. Every qualified alert MUST be recorded in the incident register.

10.2 Classification and prioritisation

10.2.1 Incidents MUST be qualified by severity:

LevelCriterionExampleTarget handling
time
P1 —
Critical		Harm to a vital asset /
proven compromise		AD compromise, chokepoint bypass,
log tampering		Immediate
P2 —
Major		Significant harm without
global compromise		Unjustified privileged container, abnormal
access to a C3 share		Within a few hours
P3 —
Minor		Localised anomalySCA configuration drift, one-off snapshot
failure		In the current cycle

10.3 Incident response

10.3.1 The response MUST follow the steps: detection → qualification → containment → eradication → recovery → closure.

10.3.2 Containment MAY rely on the pfSense chokepoint (isolating the VM concerned with a block rule), on the local firewall of the target host when the flow stays inside the segment, on disabling compromised accounts in AD, or on stopping the faulty container.

10.3.3 Recovery MUST favour a return to a known healthy state through a ZFS/Snapper snapshot or a verified backup restore (Article 8).

10.3.4 Evidence (logs, snapshots) MUST be preserved before any destructive action, as far as possible.

10.4 Lessons learned (RETEX)

10.4.1 Every P1 or P2 incident MUST lead to a documented lessons-learned review: timeline, root cause, corrective measures, and any update of the ISSP or the detection rules.

10.4.2 Corrective actions from the review MUST be followed up until closure and feed the continuous improvement cycle (Article 12).

10.5 Escalation, notification and transmission of evidence

10.5.1 Any P1 incident, or P2 incident beyond internal capabilities, MUST be escalated at once to the CISO, who decides whether to call on an ANSSI-qualified incident response provider (PRIS) and whether to report to CERT-FR.

10.5.2 When an incident is a personal data breach, the CISO MUST notify the CNIL within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (GDPR, article 33) and, where there is a high risk for the people concerned, inform them (article 34).

10.5.3 Items passed to analysts (exported logs, screenshots, snapshots) MUST come with their SHA-256 hash and a timestamped timeline; every handling (who, when, what) MUST be recorded to preserve the chain of custody.

10.5.4 Every incident MUST be entered in the incident log with its qualification, the actions taken and its closure.

Article 11 — Secrets and cryptography management

11.1 Secrets management

11.1.1 No secret or key MAY appear in clear in code, scripts, container images, versioned configuration files or logs.

11.1.2 Secrets MUST be managed through a dedicated mechanism: .env files excluded from version control with restricted rights, or, preferably, a secrets vault (Vault).

11.1.3 Secrets MUST be injected into services / containers at run time, with no clear-text persistence on disk when this can be avoided.

11.1.4 Secrets MUST be rotated regularly (at least every 90 days) and immediately on any suspicion of compromise or when a contributor leaves.

11.1.5 A secrets register (identifier, owner, use, date of last rotation — never the value) MUST be kept up to date. Secret values MUST NEVER be recorded in this register or in this ISSP.

11.2 Cryptography

11.2.1 Communications MUST be protected by TLS in its current, robust versions, or by an equivalent protocol (SSH, WireGuard); obsolete protocols and cipher suites (e.g. SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1) ARE FORBIDDEN.

11.2.2 Integrity hashes (backups, FIM checks) MUST use SHA-256 or stronger. Obsolete hash functions (MD5, SHA-1) MUST NOT be used for security purposes.

11.2.3 Private keys and certificates MUST be stored in a protected way, with restricted access, and renewed before expiry.

Article 12 — Compliance, audit and continuous improvement

12.1 Compliance

12.1.1 The compliance of the scope with this ISSP MUST be assessed at each audit cycle and at each structural change.

12.1.2 Gaps (non-compliances) MUST be recorded, rated by severity, given an action plan and an owner, and followed up until resolved.

12.2 Audit

12.2.1 Audits MUST rely on verifiable evidence: configurations, Wazuh logs, SCA/FIM reports, Grafana dashboards, registers (assets, access, secrets, exceptions, incidents) and restore tests.

12.2.2 Each audit MUST produce a dated, referenced and archived audit report (PV), listing the scope checked, the findings, the non-compliances and the recommendations. Audit reports are the lab's enforceable compliance record.

12.3 Continuous improvement cycle (PDCA)

12.3.1 Security management MUST follow the PDCA cycle:

PhasePurposeImplementation
PlanPlanRisk analysis, definition/update of rules and objectives
DoImplementApplying the measures (hardening, RBAC, logging, backup)
CheckCheckAudits, SCA/FIM, incident review, restore tests, audit reports
ActImproveCorrective actions, lessons learned, ISSP update

12.3.2 Lessons from incidents (Article 10) and audits MUST feed the update of the ISSP, which MUST be revised at least once a year.

Conclusion: the 3-2-1-0 rule is implemented in principle — in the lab, the replicated copy sits on the same pool, so the "2 media" and "1 off-site copy" criteria are only met in production (see §5) — and the restore is proven, verified and timed.

5. Limits and areas for improvement (technical honesty)

  • NFSv4 ACLs: restoring with cp produced "preserving permissions: Operation not permitted" warnings — the content is intact (SHA-256 matches), but cp does not carry the ACLs over. In production, favour a restore that preserves ACLs (rsync -A, or Windows' native "Previous Versions" exposed through SMB).
  • Real off-site copy: in this single-NAS lab, copy 3 sits on the same pool. In production, the ZFS replication task targets a remote TrueNAS on another site (the zfs send/recv mechanism demonstrated is identical).
  • Stronger immutability: consider snapshots with locked retention (ransomware protection) for copy 2.

6. Related evidence

  • Periodic TrueNAS snapshot task (screenshot).
  • Console log of the restore test (T1/T2, hashes, RTO).
  • Datasets tank/partage and tank/partage_backup (zfs list output).

Annex H · Awareness material and short training session

Project: Hybrid InfraSec — company INFRASEC

Reference: SENS-2026-01

Date: 04/10/2026 · updated on 05/10/2026 (instruction on the QR code, after INC-04)

Author: admin (secure infrastructure administrator)

Audience: INFRASEC users (office staff, remote workers) and the technical team

Framework: operational application of the ISSP — performance criterion CP9 (raise user awareness, prepare and run a short training session)

Part 1 — Short training session sheet

ItemContents
TitleGood everyday security habits
Learning objectiveAt the end, each participant can recognise a phishing email, manage a strong
password, use secure remote access and report an incident.
AudienceTwo groups: business users (awareness) and technical team (skills
development).
Duration45 minutes (30 min of content + 15 min of discussion / practical cases).
FormatIn person or by video call, projected slides + handout.
PrerequisitesNone for the user group.
Assessment5-question quiz at the end + simulated phishing exercise at D+30.
FrequencyAt hiring, then a yearly reminder and after any significant incident.

Part 2 — Awareness material (content given to users)

1. Passwords and authentication A weak password is an attacker's first way in. The INFRASEC policy (ISSP) requires:

  • a long passphrase (at least 14 characters, as the ISSP requires, ideally a string of words) rather than a short, complex word;
  • a different password per service — never the same one for email and the domain;
  • using a password manager so you neither memorise nor write them down;
  • never giving your password, even to a colleague or a "technical support" that asks for it (no legitimate service asks for it).

Remote access authentication relies on one key per device: your computer is recognised individually. The target evolution adds multi-factor authentication (MFA).

2. Phishing Phishing is still the most common attack vector. Before clicking:

  • check the real sender address (not only the displayed name);
  • be wary of urgency and threats ("your account will be suspended") — they are manipulation levers;
  • hover over a link to see the real URL before clicking; never enter your credentials from a link received by email;
  • do not open an unexpected attachment, especially executable files or documents asking you to "enable macros".

When in doubt: do not click, report it (see §5).

3. Workstation and remote access

  • Lock your session as soon as you leave your desk (clean desk, locked screen).
  • Do not plug in an unknown USB device — removable storage is disabled on the servers for this reason.
  • When working remotely, connect only through the company VPN (WireGuard) before accessing internal resources; never expose a file share on a public network.
  • The configuration QR code given at enrolment contains your secret key: read it only with the WireGuard app, never with the camera or an assistant, which may send its content to online services. If you make a mistake, tell the technical contact at once: the key will be revoked and replaced (real case handled, INC-04).
  • Lost or stolen device: report it without delay — that device's access is revoked remotely within minutes.
  • Each profile only reaches what it needs (least privilege): a denied access is not a malfunction, it is the policy.

4. Data protection (GDPR)

  • Only process personal data as part of your work and in the spaces provided (dedicated AD share).
  • Do not copy sensitive data to a personal device or an unapproved cloud service.
  • Report any suspected loss or leak of data — a GDPR incident must be qualified quickly.

5. Reporting an incident An incident reported early costs much less than an incident discovered late. What to do:

1. Do not try to "fix" it alone or erase traces.

2. Note the time, what you observed, any messages.

3. Tell the technical contact immediately (single point of contact).

4. Isolate the computer if asked (unplug the network), without switching it off if asked not to (evidence preservation).

The detection system (Wazuh SIEM) watches the infrastructure continuously: a human report complements technical detection, it does not replace it.

Part 3 — Assessment quiz (5 questions) 1. An "urgent" email from IT asks for your password for "verification". What do you do?

2. What is the difference between a good and a bad password?

3. Before accessing an internal share from home, what must you switch on?

4. You find a USB stick in the car park. What do you do?

5. You think you clicked on a phishing link. What are the first two things to do?

(Answer key given to the trainer; expected answers match §1 to §5.)

Annex I · Incident detection report and lessons learned (PV-03)

Project: Hybrid InfraSec — Zero-Trust lab

Scenario: SSH brute-force attack detected by the Wazuh SIEM

Date: 04/10/2026

Operator / analyst: admin

Detection chain: Wazuh agent (fedora) → Wazuh manager (wazuh-siem .40) → dashboard

1. Objective Demonstrate the SIEM's ability to detect, correlate and qualify a real attack, and formalise the detection → response → lessons learned chain. The exercise deliberately links the attack to a finding of audit PV-02 (F- 01) to prove the audit → risk → incident sequence.

2. Attack scenario (controlled simulation)

ItemValue
TechniqueSSH brute force / password guessing
MITRE ATT&CKT1110 (Brute Force), T1110.001 (Password Guessing), T1021.004 (Remote Services: SSH), T1078
(Valid Accounts)
Source10.10.10.2 — hypervisor administration address present on the segment (finding PV-
02 F-01)
Targetfedora (10.10.10.30), SSH service (port 22)
Load15 authentication attempts with the non-existent account hacker
Timestamp04/10/2026 at 19:17:58 CEST

Command used (attacker workstation):

for i in $(seq 1 15); do ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=3 hacker@10.10.10.30
true; done

Choosing 10.10.10.2 as the source matters: it exploits precisely the weakness found in the audit (hypervisor administration plane reachable from the production segment). The audit had therefore anticipated the attack vector.

3. Detection (Wazuh)

Single events — rule 5710 "sshd: Attempt to login using a non-existent user", level 5, agent fedora, 15 occurrences timestamped 19:17:58 (exact match with the 15 attempts sent).

Correlation — level 10 alert peak at 19:18 (Wazuh correlation rule 5712: brute force on a non-existent account, eight failures in two minutes), consolidating the repeated failures into a single high-severity event.

Automatic MITRE ATT&CK qualification — the "Threat Hunting" dashboard classifies the activity as Brute Force, Password Guessing, SSH and Valid Accounts.

Dashboard indicators (15-min window):

IndicatorValue
Authentication failures15
Alerts of level ≥ 10peak at 19:18 (brute-force correlation)
Agent concernedfedora (10.10.10.30)
Detection delayreal time (< 1 min between the attack and the alert)

Evidence: screenshots of the Threat Hunting dashboard (MITRE + level trend) and of the event list filtered on agent.name: fedora (rule 5710 ×15).

4. Incident response (procedure)

PhaseAction
IdentificationWazuh level 10 alert (SSH brute force) on fedora, source 10.10.10.2.
ContainmentBlocking the source on the target host (local firewalld on the fedora node): the
source and target are in the same segment, so the flow does not cross pfSense,
which cannot filter it. Wazuh active response (firewall-drop) automates this
block on the agent; enabling it permanently is kept as a lesson learned.
EradicationTreating the root cause: removing the administration address 10.10.10.2 from the
segment (finding F-01) is decided, then requalified at the freeze as a risk accepted temporarily
with a compensating measure, pending a dedicated administration network (measure M-
01). SSH hardening applied on the target (F-07: root login forbidden, three attempts at
most, idle timeouts, detailed logging); key-only authentication is
kept as an improvement.
RecoveryService integrity checked (no successful access — account hacker does not exist, 0
compromise); back to normal operations.
CapitalisationWriting this lessons-learned report and updating the ISSP / hardening plan.

Result: no compromise (every attempt failed on a non-existent account). The incident stayed at the attempt stage, detected in real time.

5. Lessons learned (RETEX)

What worked well

  • The detection chain is working end to end: the agent forwarded the logs, the manager correlated, the dashboard qualified the attack and mapped it onto MITRE ATT&CK — all in real time.
  • Multi-source monitoring (Wazuh SIEM + SCA + system logs) gives immediate visibility on suspicious activity.
  • The exercise validates the relevance of the audit: the vector used (F-01) had been identified and rated before the incident.

Areas for improvement identified

  • Automate the response: enable Wazuh active response to ban brute-force sources automatically (shorter reaction time).
  • Reduce the surface: restrict SSH to an administration workstation/bastion (Zero-Trust principle) and move to key-based authentication + MFA.
  • Treat the root cause: remove the hypervisor administration plane from the production segment (F-01) — priority of the freeze phase.
  • Enrich detection: add suitable rules/thresholds and dashboards dedicated to access attempts.

Main lesson An untreated audit finding (F-01) is a real, exploitable attack path. The loop audit → risk analysis (EBIOS) → detection (SIEM) → remediation (hardening) is demonstrated here completely and consistently.

6. Traceability

the hypervisor"

Annex J · Technical and security incident log

Register of the incidents met while building the lab and of their resolution. Each entry is evidence of diagnosis and technical control (CCP2 / CCP3). Sheets are numbered in the chronological order in which they occurred.

INC-01 — The installation ISO fails to boot (TrueNAS VM)

Date: 02/10/2026

Asset: VM truenas (Fedora 44 / KVM-libvirt hypervisor, managed through Cockpit)

Symptom The VM stays stuck on the OVMF firmware menu "Please select boot device"; the TrueNAS SCALE 25.10.7 ISO image does not start. In Cockpit's graphical console (noVNC), the arrow keys work but the Enter key is not passed to the virtual machine. The VM ends up stopping on its own.

Diagnosis

1. UEFI boot (OVMF) does not select the CD drive automatically despite a "CD first" boot order.

2. The web console does not reliably pass the Enter key → the highlighted entry cannot be confirmed.

3. Injecting the key from the host (virsh send-key … KEY_ENTER) fails intermittently because the VM is no longer running when the command arrives ("domain is not running").

Root cause An unfavourable combination: OVMF/UEFI firmware (firmware auto-selection + persistent NVRAM keeping a stale boot order) and the keyboard transmission limit of Cockpit's noVNC console.

Resolution Switching the VM firmware from UEFI to BIOS (SeaBIOS):

  • removal of the <firmware> block (auto-selection + secure boot), of the <loader> element and of the <nvram> element;
  • removal of the firmware='efi' attribute from the <os> section;
  • redefinition of the VM (virsh define) then start.

SeaBIOS boots the CD directly and starts the TrueNAS installer, with no intermediate menu or keyboard input needed.

Proof Screenshot of the "TrueNAS 25.10.7 Console Setup" screen obtained after the switch; timestamp 02/10/2026 12:07.

Lesson For lab VMs administered through Cockpit's web console, prefer SeaBIOS firmware when installation requires keyboard interaction in the console: booting removable media is more reliable and avoids depending on special key transmission.

INC-02 — Active Directory join fails (clock, then password)

Date: 02/10/2026

Asset: VM truenas (10.10.10.20) — join to the infrasec.local domain

Symptom 1 On validation, error: "Time offset from the domain controller exceeds the maximum permitted value". The join is refused.

Diagnosis 1 Clocks compared from the hypervisor (virsh domtime): TrueNAS has the correct UTC time; the domain controller DC01 shows a UTC offset greater than 5 minutes. Cause: the DC's time zone was set wrongly, so its effective UTC time was off. Kerberos allows a maximum offset of 5 minutes.

Resolution 1 Time zone and time corrected on DC01 (UTC+1 Paris, daylight saving on), which aligns its UTC time with real time and with TrueNAS. NTP synchronisation of the DC to the pfSense firewall (time authority of the segment) configured as well.

Symptom 2 New error: "The bind password is not correct."

Diagnosis 2 The join account password was typed on a keyboard layout different from the one used when it was set (US QWERTY vs FR AZERTY), producing a different string.

Resolution 2 Join account password reset with characters at the same position on both layouts (neutral characters), then input checked on screen.

Proof Active Directory status: HEALTHY — realm INFRASEC.LOCAL, keytab AD_MACHINE_ACCOUNT created, account cache enabled.

Lesson For any Kerberos join: (1) synchronise the time of every member on a single source (NTP from the DC or the chokepoint) before joining; (2) for multi-platform service accounts, avoid characters sensitive to the keyboard layout.

INC-03 — Windows monitoring: obsolete collectors and incompatible dashboard

Date: 04/10/2026

Asset: VM Win-Server-DC (10.10.10.10) — agent windows_exporter v0.31.8; Prometheus/Grafana server on fedora (10.10.10.30)

Context Deploying the windows_exporter metrics exporter on the domain controller for monitoring by Prometheus and display in Grafana. Installed through a script served by a temporary HTTP server (workaround for the copy-paste limitation of the noVNC web console).

Symptom 1 — service stopped After installing the MSI, the windows_exporter service stays Stopped; Start-Service returns no error but the service ends at once.

Diagnosis 1 Run in the foreground to capture the error: couldn't enable collectors" err="unknown collector cs", then unknown collector logon. The cs (computer-system) and logon collectors were removed in recent versions; the requested set contained obsolete names.

Root cause 1 Version drift: invalid collector names in windows_exporter 0.31.8. The service fails as soon as an unknown collector is requested.

Resolution 1 Self-correcting deployment script: iterative test of the collector set, automatic removal of any collector reported as "unknown", then reconfiguration of the service's ImagePath (registry) with the validated set and restart. Final set: cpu, logical_disk, net, os, service, system, memory, process, tcp, ad, dns (including ad and dns, specific to the domain controller role).

Symptom 2 — "No data" dashboard Prometheus target windows-dc is UP (26 ms scrape), but Grafana dashboard ID 14694 shows no data; the "Server" variable stays empty (warning triangle).

Diagnosis 2 Two combined causes: (a) Prometheus job named windows-dc instead of the expected windows convention; (b) dashboard 14694 (published in 2021) built on the windows_cs_* metrics provided by the now removed cs collector — so the instance variable can no longer fill in.

Resolution 2 (a) Prometheus job name aligned on windows and service reloaded. (b) Dashboard replaced by an up-to-date template, explicitly compatible with windows_exporter v0.31+ (Grafana ID 23942), with the Prometheus data source correctly bound at import.

Proof "Windows Exporter Dashboard 2025" showing all the metrics of the DC01 domain controller: CPU, memory (5.93 GiB total / 3.65 GiB free), disk space, VirtIO network, disk I/O, service state, process and thread counts.

Lesson (1) Never assume collector/metric names are stable across exporter versions; industrialise deployment with an idempotent, self-correcting script. (2) Check a community dashboard's version compatibility with the exporter version before concluding there is a configuration error. (3) Follow the job naming conventions (job) expected by the tool ecosystem.

INC-04 — Security incident: exposure of the private key of an administrator access

Date: 05/10/2026

Asset: WireGuard peer admin-remote (10.10.20.2) — remote access to the administration plane; firewall fw01

Triggering event When enrolling the smartphone, the administrator profile's configuration QR code was read with the phone's camera app instead of the WireGuard app. This code contains the full client configuration, private key included. The camera sent its content to an online visual search service: the private key left the device and was passed to a third party.

Qualification Real security incident — breach of the confidentiality of an authentication secret tied to a privileged profile (access to the administration plane). Exploitation also requires reaching the tunnel endpoint, which lowers its likelihood in the lab; the key is nonetheless treated as compromised, on the principle: an exposed secret is a compromised secret, without waiting for proof of exploitation.

Containment Immediate removal of the old public key of the admin-remote peer on the firewall: the exposed key no longer opens any tunnel, whoever holds it.

Eradication and recovery Generation of a new key pair (rotation), new public key declared on the peer, new QR code produced, enrolment redone only with the WireGuard app. Check: the handshake succeeds with the new key; the firewall no longer knows the old one.

Preservation of evidence Timeline and screenshots kept offline. No private key material — old or new — appears in any deliverable; only public keys are referenced.

Lessons learned (1) A WireGuard configuration QR code is a secret: it carries the client's private key. (2) It must only be read with the WireGuard app; camera apps and assistants may send what they read to online services. (3) Revocation by removing the public key worked as planned: requirement EF5 of the specifications (centralised, immediate revocation) is demonstrated in a real situation. (4) Organisational measure: instruction added to the awareness material and to the skills transfer. Technical measure considered: distribute the configuration as a file over an encrypted channel and show the QR code only during enrolment.

INC-05 — Remote access test skewed by the hypervisor's presence on the segment

Date: 06/10/2026

Asset: remote access test bench — hypervisor TeneT

Symptom A first test of the employee profile was run from the hypervisor, used as a WireGuard client. The connection tool refused to add the tunnel route (RTNETLINK answers: File exists) and yet the connection test to the share succeeded.

Diagnosis The hypervisor already has a direct address and route to the 10.10.10.0/24 segment — that is audit finding F-01. So the flow did not go through the tunnel: the test "succeeded" without proving anything about remote access or segmentation.

Resolution The test client was isolated in a dedicated network namespace, with no route to the internal segment: any flow to 10.10.10.0/24 must go through the tunnel. This bench validated the handshake and located the key-based routing defect (INC-06). Final end-to-end validation is done from a separate client machine on the WAN side.

Lesson (1) A remote access test must start from a machine really outside the protected network; otherwise it measures the wrong path. (2) Finding F-01 is not theoretical: here it skewed a test, just as it served as the source of the simulated attack in PV-03. It confirms the priority of measure M-01 (dedicated administration network).

INC-06 — WireGuard: data plane broken by duplicated "Allowed IPs" (cryptokey routing)

Date: 06/10/2026

Asset: firewall fw01 (pfSense CE, WireGuard package) — tunnel tun_wg0 (10.10.20.0/24), peers employe-remote (10.10.20.3) and admin-remote (10.10.20.2)

Symptom The WireGuard handshake completes correctly (bytes exchanged both ways, tunnel "green"), but no TCP connection from the remote client employe-remote (10.10.20.3) to the TrueNAS SMB share (10.10.10.20:445) succeeds: nc -zv -w3 10.10.10.20 445 always returns TIMEOUT. The packet capture on the firewall's LAN interface shows the client's SYN relayed to TrueNAS, which answers with a SYN-ACK — but that SYN-ACK is retransmitted in a loop and never goes back into the tunnel to the client.

Diagnosis

1. A working handshake rules out a key or endpoint problem.

2. The LAN capture proves the Zero-Trust filtering rule allows the flow and the destination server answers: the problem is on the firewall's return path to the tunnel.

3. Inspecting VPN → WireGuard → Peers: both peers had the same value Allowed IPs = 10.10.20.2/32. No peer "owned" the address 10.10.20.3 used by the employee client.

Root cause A cryptokey routing configuration error. In WireGuard, the server-side Allowed IPs field does two jobs: (a) an access control list (which source addresses are accepted from this peer) and (b) an internal routing table (which peer to encrypt a packet for, by destination address). Since 10.10.20.3 was declared on no peer, pfSense could not determine which peer to encrypt the returning SYN-ACK for → packet dropped. On top of that came a collision (two peers claiming 10.10.20.2), which pfSense reports explicitly: "traffic to the conflicting networks will only be routed to the last peer in the list". Since the handshake depends only on keys and endpoint, the tunnel looked healthy despite a broken data plane — a classic trap.

Resolution The Allowed IPs field of peer employe-remote corrected to 10.10.20.3/32 (peer admin- remote kept at 10.10.20.2/32), guaranteeing unique ranges between peers. Saved (Save Peer) then applied (Apply). Check on the peer list: employe-remote → 10.10.20.3/32, admin-remote → 10.10.20.2/32.

Status / reach Fix applied and checked at configuration level. The end-to-end test run from the network namespace (netns) validation bench on the hypervisor remains inconclusive, because of an asymmetry specific to the bench: the netns client's endpoint is seen by the firewall as 192.168.122.1, i.e. on the same subnet as the pfSense WAN (192.168.122.0/24), which creates a hairpin not representative of a really remote client. Representative end-to-end validation is therefore done in the acceptance test (step E8 of the go-live plan), from a separate client machine placed on the lab WAN network with no route to the internal segment outside the tunnel.

Proof Screenshots of the Peers tab before the fix (two peers at 10.10.20.2/32) and after the fix (.3/32 and .2/32); LAN packet capture showing the SYN relayed to TrueNAS and the SYN-ACK retransmitted.

Lesson (1) Distinguish the two roles of the Allowed IPs field in WireGuard: authorisation and cryptokey routing. (2) An established handshake does not prove the data plane works; always validate the application flow. (3) Allowed IPs ranges must be unique between the peers of a tunnel. (4) Choose a test bench whose topology does not reintroduce asymmetry (client endpoint outside the firewall's WAN subnet).

Update of 11/10/2026. The acceptance test run from a separate client machine (PV-04) showed that fixing the Allowed IPs was necessary but not sufficient: the same symptom remained, with a second cause on the firewall interface side (INC-07). The hypothesis of an asymmetry specific to the netns bench therefore did not, on its own, explain the failure seen on 06/10.

INC-07 — WireGuard: server replies not routed to the tunnel (WG_REMOTE interface without static addressing)

Date: 11/10/2026

Asset: firewall fw01 — assigned interface WG_REMOTE (tun_wg0), peer employe-remote (10.10.20.3)

Symptom During the acceptance test, from the dedicated client wg-client on the WAN side: handshake established (latest handshake: Now), but nc -zv -w3 10.10.10.20 445 fails (Connection timed out). The WAN-side capture shows the client sending encrypted packets every second with no answer from the firewall.

Diagnosis

1. The SMB share answers from the internal network: the TrueNAS service is not the cause.

2. The counters of the rule employe-remote → TrueNAS SMB (445) increase: the firewall allows and relays the request.

3. Capture on the firewall's LAN interface: TrueNAS answers (SYN-ACK to 10.10.20.3). TrueNAS's default gateway (10.10.10.254) is correct.

4. So the defect is located, as for INC-06, on the firewall's return path to the tunnel.

Root cause The assigned interface WG_REMOTE was configured with IPv4 addressing type "None". With no address or prefix on the interface, pfSense had no connected route to 10.10.20.0/24: the server's reply followed the default route (WAN) instead of entering the tunnel. A first fix with 10.10.20.1/32 had no effect (the /32 prefix does not cover the clients' segment).

Resolution Interface WG_REMOTE set to static IPv4 10.10.20.1/24, with no upstream gateway; state table reset. Immediate check: Connection to 10.10.10.20 445 port

[tcp/microsoft-ds] succeeded!

Proof WAN capture (encrypted packets with no answer), LAN capture (SYN-ACK present), connection successful after the fix; full acceptance test recorded in PV-04.

Lesson (1) On pfSense, the interface assigned to a WireGuard tunnel must carry the address and the prefix of the clients' segment: it is what creates the return route. (2) Two independent causes can produce the same symptom; fixing the first one (INC-06) was not proof. (3) Diagnosis by successive captures — WAN, rule, LAN — locates the failing link in a few minutes; it is the method kept for operations.

Annex K · Cybersecurity threat watch process

"Hybrid InfraSec" project — company INFRASEC

ReferenceVEI-2026-01
PurposeOrganise the watch on threats, vulnerabilities, tool changes and
regulation, and turn it into security maintenance actions and
detection rules
AuthorRJ — secure infrastructure administrator

Date11 October 2026

1. Why a structured watch An infrastructure that is secure on its go-live day is no longer secure a few months later if nothing changes around it: new vulnerabilities are published every week, attack techniques evolve, vendors change their products. The watch is the sensor that triggers security maintenance. Without it, patches arrive late and detection rules age.

The process described here answers three questions: what to watch (the scope), where to look (the sources), and what to do with what we find (the decision process and its traceability).

2. Watch scope — inventory first An effective watch starts from the inventory: an alert is only worth something if it concerns a component that is really present. The scope covers the project's assets.

administration pivot)

The choice favours primary sources — the national authority, the vendor, the reference database — rather than secondary relays, to avoid distorted or late information.

4. Process: from information to action

Collecte → Qualification → Décision → Action → Traçabilité → Diffusion

Qualification. Each piece of information is checked against the inventory (is the component present? in which version? exposed?) then rated: CVSS severity, known active exploitation (KEV catalogue, CERT-FR alert), real exposure in the architecture.

Decision. Three possible outcomes: fix (update, configuration change); apply a compensating measure until the patch is available (filtering, disabling a service, detection rule); accept the risk, with a dated justification.

Target handling times:

CriticalityCriterionTime
CriticalCVSS ≥ 9, or proven active exploitation on an
exposed component		Immediate compensating measure, patch
within 72 h
HighCVSS 7 to 8.915 days
MediumCVSS 4 to 6.9Monthly maintenance cycle
LowCVSS < 4Next planned cycle

Action and adaptation of detection. When a relevant attack technique is identified, the watch does not stop at the patch: it questions the detection capability. A Wazuh rule is created or tuned so that the technique is seen if it is attempted.

Traceability. Each piece of information kept goes into the watch register (§5). Distribution. Immediate alert to the CISO for a critical item; monthly one-page summary to management; added to the awareness material when user behaviour is involved.
